pinboard.title: The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored - The Atlantic
pinboard.description:
The conspiracy theory that persists even though no evidence supports it
For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world.
The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review, was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me.
This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy.
And yet for the past year and a half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely.
The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either.

pinboard.title: Black Mountain College Was a Mess - by Carl DiSalvo
pinboard.description:
"And also, it worked."

...

"For a while now I’ve been interested in Black Mountain College. It’s an example of a school that melded together many ways of knowledge and making through an experimental approach to learning and teaching. It’s also not too far away, in a part of the country that’s grown meaningful to me. The closeness, culture of the place, and familiarity of the landscape add to its appeal.

Over the past few years, I’ve collected and been gifted quite a pile of books on Black Mountain College. Many of them are gorgeous volumes of photographs of the school, the people, and all the things made there, and I’ve often flipped through them. But it’s only in the last year I’ve been seriously reading these books, studying Black Mountain College.

There’s no reason to be familiar with Black Mountain College, so a bit of background. The college was an experimental liberal arts school that operated from 1933 to 1957 in the Blue Ridge Mountains near the town of Black Mountain, North Carolina. It was founded by John Andrew Rice and a small group of faculty after Rice was dismissed from another college over disputes about academic freedom and his progressive educational philosophy. Together, they envisioned a school where learning would be driven by inquiry rather than rigid curricula, and where the arts would occupy a central place in a liberal education.

What’s not to love?

From the beginning, Black Mountain attracted an amazing faculty. Josef and Anni Albers arrived after the closure of the Bauhaus. They were joined by composer John Evarts and philosopher and educational theorist Theodore Dreier. Black Mountain is perhaps best remembered for the artists who passed through, including John Cage, Merce Cunningham, and Buckminster Fuller as visiting faculty, and students like Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly, and Ruth Asawa. Writers including Charles Olson, Robert Creeley, Denise Levertov, and Robert Duncan made the college an important place for American poetry.

All tucked into the hot, human, and ridiculously beautiful hills of Appalachia.

To give a sense of the learning environment…there were two divisions for students, Junior Division and Senior Division. It was up to the students to decide when they had learned enough to take the exam to move from one division to the next. The exam consisted of two days of written questions followed by an oral examination that lasted… as long as it had to. For the written exam, students were allowed to use their notes, the library, their experience, really anything they had access too. The questions weren’t limited to topics covered in courses; they were questions that tested a student’s ability to engage in investigation and analysis. Imagine being asked: “How do you know the Philippine Islands exist?” and given nine hours to discover and write-up an answer.

One of my favorite books so far is Martin Duberman’s Black Mountain: An Exploration in Community. Most of the other books I have are about the arts of Black Mountain. This one, as the title suggests, is about the community, the people who came together to found, create, and sustain, the place. It’s a massive history book, over 500 pages, and Duberman spent years interviewing folks who had been part of Black Mountain College, including faculty, visitors, and students, and pouring over all manner of documents in the archives, from faculty meeting minutes to fundraising letters.

And one of the things we learn is that Black Mountain College was a mess.

From the start, it was unstable. Finances were precarious. The buildings in the first few years were rented from a summer camp. The relationship with the nearby towns was shaky due to all manner of rumors and truths about the goings at the college (they wore sandals and rolled-up dungarees!). The cast of characters were opinionated to the point of being stubborn, and most all of them were exceptional at arguing—a dangerous combination. The courses offered depended entirely on the faculty present, their interests and abilities. Lauded progressive endeavors, such the farm work program, were tumultuous. The democratic governance of the school, for which it was renowned, was tenuous and at times served to reinforce conservative positions. The value of the education was uncertain and the college was never actually accredited. Very few students “graduated,” whatever that might mean in such an open educational context.

Perhaps none of that instability is surprising. There’s nothing about the structure of Black Mountain College that would suggest financial stability, or any kind of stability for that matter. In fact, it seems it was almost intentionally unstable, or at least, many of the things that usually provide institutional stability were purposefully omitted from its operations. Governance is often difficult, but especially so when undertaken by a group of people self-selecting against authority and routine.

In other words, a mess.

And also, it worked.

Reading through this, I’ve tried to make sense of it.

How did it work?*

Was it the extraordinary faculty? Maybe, but also, the extraordinary faculty were part of what Black Mountain College difficult, doggedly holding their educational ideologies dear and often teaching ideas that had yet to be fully thought through. Was it the democratic approach to decision making? Well, as with many democratic communities, charisma and authority were strong forces of influence. Was it freedom from familiar institutional traditions? Yes, but that that freedom also limited access to funds and made accreditation impossible.

There’s probably some organizational theory that explains this, which I just don’t know.

Here’s what I’ve come up…

It worked because they had a mess they believed in and were committed to.

Part of that belief and commitment was attending to the mess.

For folks at Black Mountain College, it wouldn’t have been enough to sit in a library are read theories of progressive education. They did the work of cultivating and sustaining those conditions. They made the school happen, and kept it open for decades. They built programs, such as the farm work program, and they debated those programs for hours over and over again, while also doing them. It was an abstract ideal, but put into steadfast practice. They were committed to doing the work of trying to learn and teach differently, because they shared the principles that motivated that work.

And, part of that belief was also a willingness to let the mess be, because there seemed to be an understanding that the mess it was necessary for the vision.

A mess without belief is a problem, and we’re often driven to clean it up, mostly for the sake of not having a mess anymore. The mess makes our work more difficult, so putting it to rights is the right thing to do because it lets us better get on to our work.

But what if the mess is the work?

For Black Mountain College, it maybe the mess was the work. It had to be relatively contained, occasionally rearranged. But it also had to remain a mess.

They weren’t careless in this. They worked incredibly hard at maintaining an institution that remained unstable but also able to be responsive when needed.

Consider grades, a basic thing in most colleges. At Black Mountain College they did away with grades (of course). But also they also kept a record of grades so, if needed, students could have transcripts. One can imagine the exchange…

Student: “Am I passing my courses?”
College: “That’s the wrong question.”
Graduate School: “We need the student’s grades.”
College: “Oh, we have those.”
Student: “What are they?”
College: “Don’t worry, they’re not important.”

Over twenty-some years, the faculty and students of Black Mountain College could have made all sorts of decisions that would have made the operations of more orderly. But they didn’t.

It was methodical, but it wasn’t efficient.

Digging a ditch, drawing with Josef Albers, milking a cow, taking “Group Dynamics” with John Wallen, debating admissions policy in a hours long meeting, participating in a theatre production of No Exit, reading towards your research…all could be in in week’s work at Black Mountain College, maybe while paying tuition, maybe not, maybe your contract for teaching would be renewed, maybe not. But you would learn, in a Black Mountain College sort of way.

What seemed to make it work, for lack of a better word, was faith: a confidence and devotion to the shared endeavor.

This is the tension that ken wrote about last week.

It’s not being in a mess that’s a problem.

The problem is being in a mess that you don’t believe in.

But a mess you believe in. That can be brilliant.

---

Image Credit: From the Black Mountain College Research Project Papers, Visual Materials, North Carolina State Archives, Raleigh, NC.

---

* One could argue that it didn’t work because it’s not still a school, it eventually closed (and that’s another part of the story). But it did run for over twenty years, with more than a 1000 people involved and affected, nurtured some of the most influential creatives of the twentieth century, spawned many books, articles, exhibitions, and continues to be inspirational today. So, as far as I’m concerned, something about it, in some way, worked. In fact, it’s still working."

pinboard.title: How "ghost creators" cashed in on America’s divided politics • Semafor
pinboard.description:
Max Tani:

“William,” a middle-aged man in a blue short-sleeved button-down shirt whose YouTube videos have more than 14 million views, looked straight into the camera at his kitchen table in August and read a script about New York City’s mayor. His video, Mayor Mamdani Panics as Taylor Swift Triggers a $2.3 Billion Celebrity Exodus, quickly racked up more than 474,000 views. “Omar,” a shaggy, bearded creator who claimed to be based in New York, read a report to viewers in June about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and her ex. AOC FREAKS OUT as Riley Roberts CAUGHT Running Her ENTIRE Operation, set to ominous music, got more than 250,000 views. The same music played on a video, Socialist Seattle Mayor CRIES As A Beloved Bookstore Closes, from a channel called Julian News Report. It also registered a quarter of a million views. To the casual YouTube viewer, these would look like unconnected videos from political news creators outraged by events happening in cities led by Democrats. The reality is more complicated. “William” and “Omar” are actors, Semafor found in a forensic accounting of their channels’ origins. They were reading formulaic, repetitive scripts that appeared to be generated or aided by large-language models. Over the last several months, a new generation of YouTube growth-hackers have flooded American politics with sensationalized, low-quality content, reaching millions of viewers with nearly identical videos taking aim at progressive politicians including Zohran Mamdani, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Notably, while the videos are presented as laypeople giving straight-to-camera ideological news recaps, they feature actors and spokespeople paid small amounts of money to read nearly identical scripts laced with misleading claims and outright falsehoods. Viewers either didn’t notice or didn’t mind: A single network of interconnected videos that are affiliated with a growth-hacking company whose founder promises to be the “strongest alternative to paid ads” garnered well over 45 million views and 90,000 comments on YouTube as well as millions more impressions across social platforms like TikTok. With that level of viral videos, a small media organization can make tens or even hundreds of thousands a month.

Marina Hyde mentioned a theory that all algorithmic feeds are fake these days. This feels like more confirmation of that.

Rob Waugh:

Press Gazette has raised questions about four more prolific finance journalists who have so far been unable to verify their identities and have written for a number of well-known journalism brands. The new investigation follows Press Gazette’s report into four other finance journalists who together have more than 1,000 published articles and who, three months on, have not come forward to verify that they exist. Again the questionable freelances have a history of writing positive stories about cryptocurrency launches and some appear to be linked to leading PR outlets for the blockchain industry Inbound Junction and Market Across.  Two of the four new journalists are highlighted in case studies on the website of Israel-based Inbound Junction, and several promote coins linked to the agency including the controversial Gladius coin which collapsed, losing investors money. The four have appeared in top finance publications including Forbes, Entrepreneur, Information Age and The Next Web. Press Gazette asked publications who have published work by the four to verify their credentials and none have been able to do so. All four have thin online profiles and few ways to contact them. After being contacted by Press Gazette, Hacker Noon and Information Age have removed articles by the journalists. Sadie Ann Williamson has had dozens of pieces published online, including in Entrepreneur, Hackernoon, IB Times, Venturebeat and Information Age. Williamson bills herself as a blockchain expert, with a company called Williamson Fintech Consulting based in New Zealand – but its address on Quay Street is in a retail area, and no company of that name is listed in Google Maps.

Cryptocurrency and fake journalists? Shocked, I tell you, shocked.

pinboard.title: The car industry A/B tested selling a car with and without CarPlay and the results are not shocking
pinboard.description:
A couple years ago, GM made waves by saying that soon, all their new cars would be completely free of Apple's CarPlay and Android Auto support, instead opting for the "Android Automotive OS" in their cars.
Admittedly, I'm a huge fan of CarPlay for basic safety reasons and how it lets you hear or send texts without ever having to look at or touch your phone, so I was not happy to hear this news. I remember when this was first announced for Chevy EVs and when it was later expanded to all their cars in the future and the resounding response was that car buyers were PISSED.
Chevy claimed they were doing this for privacy reasons, that none of your driving or phone data would go to Apple any longer, but instead it would all go to Google (who would likely share it with General Motors, the owners of Chevy).
Chevy seemed to ignore the uproar from their fans and went ahead with it anyway, and as far as I can tell, all 2025 Chevy electric vehicles shipped with the Android Auto OS and don't interface with your phone beyond bluetooth or let you see CarPlay or AndroidAuto apps on your dash...
...Give consumers a choice, and they'll take the best option
Drivers want more options for how they interact with their devices, and they are increasingly preferring to buy a Chevy covered in Honda badges that comes with phone integrations instead of buying the actual Chevy the Honda is based on, which lacks it.
I wonder if Chevy will ever backpedal from their choice to remove CarPlay and Android Auto? Drivers seem to be voting with their dollars on the question, and they're voting favorably in one direction on this issue.
Now that the market has spoken loud and clear, will General Motors listen?
(This post inspired by a toot my pal Pat wrote months ago that made me want to look up the latest sales figures today)
